newsitem.title: FRANCE: Stocks plunge, Juppe teeters on shock French vote.
newsitem.headline: Stocks plunge, Juppe teeters on shock French vote.

text.p: French stocks plunged on Monday and Prime Minister Alain Juppe hinted President Jacques Chirac may have to replace him after the left-wing opposition outpolled his centre-right coalition in a parliamentary election first round.

The Paris Bourse opened 3.84 percent down and briefly shed more than four percent as anxious traders weighed the risk of an upset left-wing victory in next Sunday's decisive runoff round, a prospect that financial markets had widely ignored until now.

By 0900 GMT, after an hour's trading, the CAC-40 blue chip share index had steadied somewhat to be 2.65 percent down. The franc slipped to 3.3773 per mark in early trading but recovered to 3.3752, less than a centime lower than last Friday's close.

The morning after his RPR-UDF alliance suffered a stinging rebuff from voters, Juppe said he was convinced Chirac would make the right choice if a change of personality were needed for the centre-right coalition to win the election.

"If the sole obstacle to the modernisation and renovation of France is a choice of personality, I am quite convinced the president will know how to make the right choice," he told reporters in Bordeaux, where a Socialist challenger forced him into a runoff in his adopted constituency.
Responding to veiled calls for his removal, the prime minister said: "What is at stake is not Alain Juppe but France."
Whatever the outcome of next Sunday's second round, he said, his government would tender its resignation to Chirac, in line with French tradition.
His comments were the nearest he has come to acknowledging that the president may have to sacrifice him to salvage the coalition after the left's strong first round vote.

With almost all votes from metropolitan France counted, the Interior Ministry said the combined left had polled 40.15 percent of the vote, the centre-right RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate rightists 36.45 percent and the extreme-right National Front 15.06 percent. Ecologists scored 6.86 percent.
Polling institutes said the result threw the outcome of the second round wide open, with the left projected to win a wafer-thin overall majority if Sunday's pattern were repeated.

Much will depend on how National Front supporters vote in the roughly 490 constituencies where their candidate failed to qualify for the runoff, and on whether the right can mobilise some of the 31.7 percent of voters who abstained.
National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, who called on Chirac to resign after Sunday's massive protest vote, was due to announce his position on the second round later on Monday.
Juppe's fellow Gaullist rival, outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, hinted it might be time to change premiers given Sunday's election warning.
As the right licked its wounds, Seguin, France's best-known Eurosceptic, forecast on RTL radio that the coalition would end up at best with a five or six-seat majority.

"You don't change campaign leaders in mid-watch, but given that one of the best hypotheses is that the centre-right could win a majority of a few seats, the problems at stake are different from those posed by a hundred-seat advance," he said.
Former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, also an RPR member, said that to make Juppe the sole issue in the first round result would be missing the point.
"Looking for a scapegoat would not allow us to find the true answers to the citizens' discontent. The ruling coalition as a whole has been taught a lesson," he told France-Inter radio.

The left pledged vigorous state job-creation measures and a shorter working week without loss of pay to attack record 12.8 percent unemployment. The coalition promised market reforms to scale down state control, cut taxes and free private enterprise.
Ministers have acknowledged a "warning" across the government's bows in a protest vote against two years of austerity, high taxes and rising unemployment.
The vote put pressure on Chirac to intervene again in the election, in which he gambled his presidency 10 months before his giant parliamentary majority needed to face voters.

"Naming a new prime minister would appear like capitulation to the enemy," said political commentator Alain Duhamel. "Chirac could however give two or three personalities a more prominent role, like (former premier) Edouard Balladur or Seguin."
Socialist ex-labour minister Martine Aubry played down the risk of conflict on domestic or European policy if France was forced into a new bout of "cohabitation", or power-sharing.
"If France chooses a leftist majority...I'm convinced Chirac will follow the trend set by France and the majority of the French people. I don't see any great difficulties," she said.
